<design_philosophy>
You are building ONE web page whose only job is to let a reader understand a research paper faster
than they could by opening the PDF. Every decision on the page is judged against that.

WHAT "FASTER" MEANS HERE
- A reader who leaves after thirty seconds still knows the finding and the number behind it.
- A reader who stays five minutes has the method, the figures and the caveats, in that order.
- Nothing on the page is there because a layout had a slot for it.

ACCURACY IS THE HARD CONSTRAINT
Every number, name and claim comes from the paper as written — you read them out of the LaTeX
source, the only source this page has. You never change a number's precision, never restate a
comparison the paper did not make, and never invent a headline figure to fill a card. A page that
looks excellent and misreports one result is worse than no page, because the PDF beside it says
something else and a reader will find that out.

CRAFT, AND THE LOOK TO AVOID
The failure mode for a generated page is a look every reader now recognises on sight: a
purple-to-blue gradient banner, three identical cards with emoji headings, and body text set in
one weight at one size. Avoid all of it.
- Type carries the design. One system font stack, a real scale with visible jumps between levels
  rather than a creep of similar sizes, long-form text around 17-19px with a measure of 65-75
  characters and generous line height. Weight and size do the emphasis; colour rarely does.
- Colour is restrained. A light, near-white ground, one dark ink for text, one accent used for
  links and the current-section marker and almost nothing else. No gradients as decoration.
- Space does the work that borders and boxes would do badly. Sections separated by real vertical
  rhythm, cards defined by alignment and a single hairline rather than by shadow stacks.
- Structure over ornament: no emoji as section markers, no icon fonts, no badge clutter, no
  animated counters.
- Motion is a courtesy. A short transition on a lightbox or a hover state is welcome; anything
  that moves on scroll, autoplays, or delays the reader is not — and all of it stops under
  prefers-reduced-motion.
- Every interactive element works with a keyboard and says what it is to a screen reader. That is
  part of the craft, not a checklist bolted on at the end.

FINISH IT
The page is done when you have opened it in a browser, read it at a phone width and a desktop
width, tabbed through every control, and found nothing to fix. Not before.
</design_philosophy>

removal, abliteration, safety fine-tuning reversal, or anything whose effect is a model that
refuses less on harmful requests), report the findings as MEASUREMENTS and their implications
for EVALUATION and DEFENCE, never as operational advice for defeating safeguards.
- State what was measured, on what, and how large the effect was, as in any other result.
- Draw the implications for the people who build and test safeguards: what an evaluation misses,

</safeguard_research_reporting>

<page_structure>
In this order, top to bottom:

1. HERO — the paper's title, the author line as the paper gives it, and a one-paragraph TL;DR in
   plain language: what was asked, what was found, and the single number that carries the finding.
   Not the abstract, and not a rewrite of it. Below it, every link the links section below
   lists, each at the exact URL given there.
2. CONTRIBUTIONS — the paper's actual contributions as three to five scannable cards, each a short
   heading plus one or two sentences. If the paper claims four things, show four cards, not five.
3. METHOD — a walkthrough a technically literate non-specialist can follow: what goes in, what
   happens to it, what comes out, and why the design is the way it is. Lead with the paper's own
   method figure when it has one.
4. RESULTS — the paper's real headline numbers, read out of `paper.tex`, each next to what it was measured on and what it is being compared against.
   A number that is not in the paper does not go on the page, and neither does a comparison the
   paper did not make. If a slot has no number, drop the slot.
5. FIGURE GALLERY — every figure, each with its caption, click-to-enlarge into a lightbox that
   closes on Escape, on a click outside, and on a visible close control.
6. LIMITATIONS — what the paper says it does not show. Verbatim in substance; do not soften it.
7. FOOTER — every link from the links section again, and the citation if the paper carries one.

A sticky section navigation runs alongside all of it and marks where the reader currently is.
Do NOT write its highlighting yourself: hand-written ones kept a stale section lit after a jump
back to the top, or never reached the short last sections. Instead give the nav element a
`data-scrollspy` attribute, make each of its links `href="#<id of that section>"`, style the
current link through `a.active` (it also gets `aria-current`), and paste this script VERBATIM
into the page's script element at the end of the body. It lights the section in view, the last one once the page is
scrolled to its end, and nothing while the reader is above the first linked section:

```js
/* aii-scroll-spy v1: paste verbatim */
(function () {
  var links = [], targets = [];
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-scrollspy] a[href^="#"]').forEach(function (a) {
    var el = document.getElementById(a.getAttribute('href').slice(1));
    if (el) { links.push(a); targets.push(el); }
  });
  if (!links.length) return;
  var queued = false;
  function current() {
    var view = window.innerHeight;
    var doc = document.documentElement;
    var atEnd = window.scrollY > 0 && view + window.scrollY >= doc.scrollHeight - 2;
    var line = atEnd ? view - 1 : Math.min(view * 0.3, 200);
    var best = null, bestTop = -Infinity;
    targets.forEach(function (el) {
      var top = el.getBoundingClientRect().top;
      if (top <= line && top > bestTop) { best = el; bestTop = top; }
    });
    return best;
  }
  function update() {
    queued = false;
    var el = current();
    links.forEach(function (a, i) {
      var on = targets[i] === el;
      a.classList.toggle('active', on);
      if (on) a.setAttribute('aria-current', 'location');
      else a.removeAttribute('aria-current');
    });
  }
  function schedule() {
    if (!queued) { queued = true; window.requestAnimationFrame(update); }
  }
  window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true });
  window.addEventListener('resize', schedule);
  window.addEventListener('load', schedule);
  if (window.ResizeObserver) new ResizeObserver(schedule).observe(document.body);
  update();
})();
```
</page_structure>

<technical_requirements>
- ONE file. All CSS in a style element, all JavaScript in a script element, both inline in
  `index.html`. No build step, no bundler, no framework, no external script, stylesheet, web
  font or analytics — nothing fetched at load time. The page must render with the network off,
  and the only local files it may point at are the figures listed above; the PDF is linked at
  its full URL, never by its local name.
- A complete HTML document: the file opens with exactly this markup, then the title and the
  style element, and closes head before the body. The viewport tag is what makes a phone lay the
  page out at its own width; without it the page renders 980px wide and shrinks to tiny text.
```html
<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```
- System font stack only, since no font may be downloaded.
- Light theme. Responsive from a 360px phone to a wide desktop, with no horizontal page scroll;
  wide content scrolls inside its own container.
- Honour prefers-reduced-motion: under it, transitions and any scroll-driven effect stop.
- Keyboard-navigable: every control reachable by Tab in a sensible order, a visible focus ring,
  the lightbox trapping focus while open and returning it to the thumbnail on close, and a skip
  link to the main content.
- Semantic HTML: one top-level heading, headings that descend without skipping, landmark elements,
  and alt text on every image that says what the figure shows rather than repeating its number.
- No emoji anywhere. No purple-to-blue gradients. No decorative icon fonts.
- Keep the whole file comfortably under a megabyte.
</technical_requirements>

<writing_register>
Write in the register of the field's best papers (the paper this page presents, which was written to them), not in the register of a language
model. Four things are measured on the finished draft, and a draft outside them is sent back with
the numbers:
- Never use: delve, underscore, showcase, intricate, pivotal, realm, commendable, meticulous, tapestry, garner, multifaceted, it is worth noting, plays a crucial role, not only ... but also. These are 10 to 30 times more frequent in machine-written abstracts than in
  human ones, and reviewers read them as such.
- Em dashes: at most 3 per 1,000 words. Use a comma, a colon or a full stop.
- Sentence rhythm: mix short and long sentences. An interquartile range of sentence length under
  8 words reads as machine-written.
- Hedging: at most 15 hedges (may, likely, suggests, appears) per 1,000
  words. State what the evidence supports plainly; hedge where it is thin, not everywhere.
Style never changes substance: numbers, claims, citations and figure markers stay exactly as the
evidence gives them. The user's original request (delivered as a separate message) overrides all
of this wherever the two conflict.
</writing_register>

The timelines and bars in (c) and (d) are schematic and carry no data values.}\n  \\label{fig:overview}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Methods}\n\\label{sec:methods}\n\n\\subsection{Data}\n\\label{sec:data}\n\n\\paragraph{Concept pool.} We assembled an outcome-blind pool of 426 emerging scientific concepts, where\noutcome-blind means that the inclusion criteria and frame were frozen and SHA-256-hashed before any\npost-appearance data were inspected. Concepts are noun-phrase surface forms that first appeared in\nOpenAlex~\\citep{Priem2022} titles and abstracts between 2005 and 2016, with 20 to 300 papers in the\nfirst-appearance window and no more than 8,000 total works through 2024.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-1/dataset-1}}\nOf the 426, 366 are main emerging concepts (247 Screen, 119 Held-out, split by a SHA-1 hash on concept\nidentifiers) and 60 are stationary reference concepts. A logistic-regression classifier trained on\nsilver-standard labels (F1 $= 0.82$ on 300 test items, AUC $= 0.89$) and a variant merger (B-cubed\nF1 $= 0.78$) were applied to ground every concept.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/experiment-1}}\nThe pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science concepts sourced from arXiv.\nFor the Screen fold, 202 concepts survive grounding filters; for the Held-out fold, 100.\n\n\\paragraph{MeSH check population.} An independent biomedical arm of 191 concepts was drawn from new MeSH\ndescriptors (DateEstablished 2006 to 2016, widened to 2004--2005 and 2017--2018), surviving a provenance\nfilter, a PubMed novelty pre-screen and the same early-volume rule. Only approximately 25\\% of new MeSH\ndescriptors are genuinely new concepts; the remainder are reclassifications or splits.\n\n\\paragraph{Works.} The combined corpus comprises 462,812 unique OpenAlex works with 488,078 verified\nconcept--work links, spanning 2000 to 2024.\n\n\\paragraph{Co-word network.} From a design-weighted whole-science background sample of 259,716 works, we\nbuilt 25 yearly three-year-window co-occurrence snapshots (approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges per\nsnapshot), with association-strength edge weights~\\citep{Nees2009}, Leiden community\ndetection~\\citep{Traag2018} (best of five seeds) and alluvial community identifiers.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/experiment-3}}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-nativeness profiles.} For each concept-keyword node, we retrieved exact OpenAlex\nsubfield-by-time-block publication counts, covering 78.7\\% of host co-occurrence weight across 1,372 nodes.\nThese profiles supply the host-vocabulary share used in RQ2. Figure~\\ref{fig:network} shows a snapshot of the\nresulting network.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig2_v0.jpg}\n  \\caption{Schematic co-word network snapshot (2012, three-year window). Nodes are concept-keyword terms\n  and grey edges are association-strength weighted co-occurrences; node fill colour marks Leiden community\n  membership, and larger circles are high-degree hub terms. Background terms (plain nodes) form dense\n  communities joined by a few inter-community edges. Pool concepts (bold black rings) sit on the periphery\n  of communities, mostly in the gaps between two of them, where they act as bridge or connector nodes; three\n  are labelled as examples (\\emph{wireless backhaul}, \\emph{EPR steering}, \\emph{holographic QCD}). The full\n  network comprises approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges; the panel is an illustrative rendering of\n  its high-degree core for readability.}\n  \\label{fig:network}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsection{Structural precursors of emergence}\n\\label{sec:rq1method}\n\n\\paragraph{Emergence labels.} We defined sustained uptake as a concept-year reaching at least 20 papers per\nyear and gaining at least 20 percentile points in co-word network strength relative to the focal population.\nThe focal-population label was declared before outcomes were computed.\n\n\\paragraph{Matched event study.} For each concept showing sustained uptake, we matched it to a control concept\nfrom the same first-appearance band and origin field that did not show sustained uptake, using 1:1\nnearest-neighbour matching on pre-period network indicators. The standardised mean difference (Cohen's $S$)\nbetween treated and control concepts at lags $k = -3$ to $0$ is the estimand. Bootstrap confidence intervals\n($B = 2{,}000$) and Holm-corrected $p$-values control for multiple testing. The Screen fold (202 concepts)\nproduced 68 onsets and 26 matched pairs.\n\n\\paragraph{Openness measures.} To test whether pre-emergence closure is reducible to neighbourhood turnover\nor Burt brokerage, we computed four variants: (a) turnover-residualised closure, obtained by regressing\nclosure on the new-relation rate, novelty, Baselga beta-similarity, log volume, concept age and Shannon\nentropy; (b) persistent-neighbour closure, restricting the closure coefficient to the top-20 neighbours\npresent in both year $y$ and $y{-}1$; (c) Burt constraint and effective size of the weighted ego\nnetwork~\\citep{Burt2004}; and (d) cross-community pair excess, defined as the count of partner pairs from\ndistinct Leiden communities minus the count expected under a strength-decile null.\n\n\\subsection{Host-entry grafting}\n\\label{sec:rq2method}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-entry events.} A host-entry event is the first year in which a concept appears in a\nnon-origin subfield together with at least five co-occurring partner terms. From 4,177 main-arm host entries,\nthe Screen fold retains 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters after the partner-count filter.\n\n\\paragraph{Exposure variable.} Host-vocabulary share (denoted $A_\\text{cont}$ in tables) is the tag-weighted\nmean of each partner's pre-entry publication share in the host subfield, where tag-weighted means that each\nco-occurrence edge is weighted by its association strength. The continuous measure is primary because only\n1.1\\% of partner tags have a host share above 50\\%. Co-transfer (denoted CT in tables) is the fraction of\npartners that were origin companions of the concept in the five years before entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Outcome.} Five-year newcomer uptake: the count of host-subfield papers by author-disjoint newcomers\n(authors with no prior concept paper and no co-authorship with concept authors) during the five years after entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Model.} Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML) regression~\\citep{Silva2006} with\nconcept-clustered standard errors~\\citep{Cameron2015}. Two specifications were pre-registered. The primary\nspecification includes concept-by-entry-year and host-by-entry-year fixed effects. The co-primary specification\nincludes concept, entry-year and host fixed effects and was declared for use when the primary drops below 30\nconcept clusters (which it does on the Held-out fold). Both specifications include co-transfer as a second\nregressor.\n\n\\paragraph{Held-out fold.} 93 concepts, 1,100 entries; minimum detectable effect (co-primary): IRR per\nstandard deviation of 1.15. The fold was used during pipeline development (event counts, population sizes and\ngating decisions were computed on both folds), so its grafting estimate is a development-set estimate, not a\ntrue held-out confirmation.\n\n\\paragraph{MeSH replication.} The same analysis was applied to 191 MeSH concepts. Because the pre-declared\npartner-count rule yielded only 192 events, the pre-declared relaxation was triggered, producing 2,171 events\nacross 160 concept clusters.\n\n\\subsection{Post-confirmation decomposition}\n\\label{sec:decomposition}\n\nAfter the Held-out and MeSH tests confirmed the host-vocabulary effect, three exploratory decompositions were\npre-specified and frozen before any coefficient was read:\n\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item \\textbf{Extensive versus intensive margins.} A linear probability model for whether any newcomer uptake\noccurs (extensive margin), and PPML conditional on uptake having started (intensive margin). Inverse-variance\nweighting (IVW) pools estimates across the Screen, Held-out and MeSH folds.\n\n\\item \\textbf{Host-specific versus generic accessibility.} Generality proxies (tag-weighted normalised subfield\nentropy and log block frequency of each partner) are added as controls. The Balassa-index lift\nmeasure~\\citep{Balassa1965}, defined as the log ratio of the host-vocabulary share to the partner's baseline\nsubfield share, is tested as an alternative exposure variable.\n\n\\item \\textbf{Origin-field dependence.} A Wald test of equality across origin-field groups (Physics and\nAstronomy, Computer Science, other).\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{Structural precursors of emergence}\n\\label{sec:rq1results}\n\n\\subsubsection{Closure measures}\n\nOn the Screen fold, concepts that later show sustained uptake have lower general closure in the years before\nonset (matched event study $S = -0.44$, 95\\% CI $-0.81$ to $-0.05$; pooled panel $S = -0.74$, 95\\% CI $-1.06$\nto $-0.46$). The pre-registered positive sign was not observed; the effect runs in the opposite direction.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Closure on the Held-out fold (development-set estimate).}\n\\label{tab:closure}\n\\footnotesize\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{X c c c c l}\n\\toprule\nMeasure & Screen $S$ & HO $S$ & HO 95\\% CI & HO Holm $p$ & Status \\\\\n\\midrule\nGeneral closure (pooled) & $-0.66$ & $-0.39$ & $-0.86$ to $0.07$ & 0.147 & Not confirmed \\\\\nTurnover-residualised & $-0.40$ & $-0.11$ & $-0.56$ to $0.34$ & 0.635 & Not confirmed \\\\\nPersistent-neighbour & $-1.12$ & $-1.07$ & $-1.86$ to $-0.29$ & 0.015 & Confirmed \\\\\nBurt constraint & $+0.08$ & $+0.11$ & $0.02$ to $0.19$ & --- & Positive \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\multicolumn{6}{l}{\\scriptsize HO = Held-out fold.}\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:closure} and Figure~\\ref{fig:closure} summarise these results. On the Held-out fold (a\ndevelopment-set estimate; the fold was used in pipeline development), general closure is not significant\n(Holm $p = 0.147$). Only persistent-neighbour closure, restricted to top-20 neighbours present in consecutive\nyears, is significant ($S = -1.07$, Holm $p = 0.015$). Burt constraint has the same positive sign on the\nHeld-out fold ($+0.11$, 95\\% CI 0.02 to 0.19), indicating that the lower closure before emergence is not\nBurt brokerage: concepts that later emerge sit in ego networks that are more constrained, not less.\n\nThe MeSH replication is directional under a sensitivity label ($D = -0.42$, Holm $p = 0.039$, $n = 29$),\nsame sign as the main pool, but under the primary label the MeSH effect is null ($D = -0.09$, Holm\n$p = 0.677$, $n = 15$).%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/experiment-4}}\n\nStructural precursors add no predictive value for whether a concept will later show sustained uptake beyond\nfrequency, burst, degree and entropy baselines (logistic AUC 0.89 versus 0.88, delta $-0.010$, 95\\% CI\n$-0.045$ to 0.021).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig3_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Pre-emergence closure on the held-out fold, by measure type. Each row shows the standardised mean\n  difference ($S$) between concepts that later show sustained uptake and matched controls. Points are estimates\n  and horizontal bars are 95\\% bootstrap confidence intervals. The dashed vertical line marks no effect\n  ($S = 0$), and Holm-corrected $p$-values are listed to the right of the first three rows. Only\n  persistent-neighbour closure (blue) survives Holm correction ($S = -1.07$, 95\\% CI $[-1.86, -0.29]$,\n  Holm $p = 0.015$). General closure (Holm $p = 0.147$) and turnover-residualised closure\n  (Holm $p = 0.635$) are shown in grey: they do not survive confirmation, and their intervals cross zero. Burt\n  constraint (orange) is positive ($S = 0.11$, 95\\% CI $[0.02, 0.19]$), which indicates that emerging concepts\n  sit in more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks.}\n  \\label{fig:closure}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\subsubsection{Comparison to related work}\n\\label{sec:rq1comparison}\n\nThe finding that emerging concepts show lower closure among their most stable co-word neighbours is consistent\nwith the observation of \\citet{Salatino2018} that new topics arise at the intersection of weakly connected\nparent areas, and with \\citeauthor{Chen2009}'s~\\citeyearpar{Chen2009} theory of structural variation in which\ntransformative work bridges structural holes. It is also consistent with the structural-holes\nliterature~\\citep{Burt2004}: concepts that later emerge connect across Leiden communities, and their\ncross-community pair excess is positive. The critical difference is that Burt constraint is higher, not lower.\nIn Burt's framework, brokerage means low constraint. Here the ego network is more redundant, not less; the\nopenness is confined to the top of the neighbourhood, while the broader ego network is dense. This pattern is\ncloser to what \\citet{Lin2021} describe as disconnection and discordance enabling new directions in science,\nand to \\citeauthor{Larson2017}'s~\\citeyearpar{Larson2017} finding that weak-tie diffusion in networks is not\nguaranteed to carry novel information.\n\nAmong Applied Network Science contributions, \\citet{Domenico2016} studied knowledge diaspora through\nsource-sink author flows, and \\citet{Cunningham2022} mapped author multidisciplinarity and disciplinary roles\nin field-of-study networks, finding that bridge authors between communities can accelerate knowledge transfer.\nOur structural analysis complements this by showing that concept-level network openness, not author-level\nbridging, precedes emergence. \\citet{Fontaine2023} traced the epistemic integration of AI into neuroscience,\nshowing how vocabulary overlap between fields facilitates absorption, a finding that connects directly to our\nhost-vocabulary result. \\citet{Doonan2019} found that community structure in co-inventor networks affects\ntime to first citation, paralleling our finding that community position shapes concept uptake.\n\\citet{Salatino2019} applied their Computer Science Ontology to classify research topics through network-based\ndetection, providing a taxonomy-grounded approach related to our co-word-network construction.\n\n\\subsection{Host-entry grafting}\n\\label{sec:rq2results}\n\n\\subsubsection{Experimental setup}\n\\label{sec:rq2setup}\n\nThe host-entry sample for the Screen fold comprises 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters (co-primary\nspecification). Entry is predominantly a package: 70\\% of partner tags are non-native origin companions, and\nonly 1.8\\% are native grafts (host share above 50\\%). The mean host-vocabulary share is 0.043 (SD 0.055). The\nHeld-out fold has 972 events across 74 concept clusters. The MeSH population has 2,171 events across 160\nconcept clusters.\n\n\\subsubsection{Main result}\n\\label{sec:rq2main}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Host-entry grafting: pre-registered test. IRR/SD = incidence-rate ratio per one standard deviation\nof host-vocabulary share. CT = co-transfer. G = concept clusters. IVW = inverse-variance weighted.}\n\\label{tab:grafting}\n\\small\n\\begin{tabularx}{\\linewidth}{l l c c c c c c}\n\\toprule\nSpecification & Fold & IRR/SD & 95\\% CI & $p$ & CT $p$ & $N$ & $G$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nCo-primary & Screen & 1.30 & 1.16--1.45 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & 0.48 & 1,544 & 140 \\\\\nCo-primary & Held-out & 1.19 & 1.06--1.33 & 0.004 & 0.60 & 972 & 74 \\\\\nPrimary (strict FE) & Held-out & 0.98 & 0.70--1.37 & 0.91 & 0.22 & 250 & 30 \\\\\nCo-primary & MeSH & 1.23 & 1.12--1.36 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & 0.053 & 2,171 & 160 \\\\\nPrimary & MeSH & 1.32 & 1.10--1.60 & 0.004 & 0.46 & 1,004 & 122 \\\\\nCo-primary (IVW) & All three & 1.26 & 1.17--1.36 & ${<}\\,0.001$ & --- & --- & --- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabularx}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:grafting} presents the pre-registered test. On the independent MeSH biomedical population, a\none-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share raises newcomer uptake by 23\\% (co-primary IRR 1.23,\n95\\% CI 1.12 to 1.36, $p < 0.001$; primary IRR 1.32, 95\\% CI 1.10 to 1.60, $p = 0.004$; pre-registered\nverdict: REPLICATED). The main-arm folds, both used in\npipeline development (event counts, population sizes and gating decisions were computed on both folds before\noutcomes were read), give concordant development-set estimates: Screen co-primary IRR 1.30 (95\\% CI 1.16 to\n1.45); Held-out co-primary IRR 1.19 (95\\% CI 1.06 to 1.33, wild-cluster bootstrap $p = 0.012$,\nnativeness-permutation $p = 0.026$). Heterogeneity between Screen and Held-out is not significant\n($p = 0.25$). The inverse-variance weighted pooled estimate across all three folds is 1.26 (95\\% CI 1.17\nto 1.36, $I^2 = 0$). Co-transfer is null across all folds and specifications\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:grafting}).\n\nThe fully saturated primary specification on the Held-out fold is inconclusive (IRR 0.98, 95\\% CI 0.70 to\n1.37) because it retains only 250 of 972 events with 30 concept clusters; this was declared underpowered in\nadvance (minimum detectable effect IRR 1.30).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig4_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Host-vocabulary effect on five-year newcomer uptake across folds and specifications. Each row gives\n  the PPML incidence-rate ratio (IRR) per one standard deviation of host-vocabulary share, on a log axis;\n  horizontal bars are 95\\% concept-clustered confidence intervals, and the dashed vertical line marks\n  IRR $= 1$ (no effect). Filled circles are the co-primary specification (concept, entry-year and host fixed\n  effects) and open circles the primary specification with concept$\\times$year and host$\\times$year fixed\n  effects. Blue marks the OpenAlex screen and sealed held-out folds, green the independent MeSH replication,\n  and the amber diamond the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) pooled co-primary estimate. The co-primary effect\n  is significant on all three folds (screen IRR 1.30 [1.16, 1.45], held-out 1.19 [1.06, 1.33], MeSH 1.23\n  [1.12, 1.36]), and the pooled estimate is 1.26 [1.17, 1.36]. The primary specification is inconclusive on\n  the held-out fold (IRR 0.98 [0.70, 1.37], 30 clusters, $p = 0.91$) but significant on MeSH (IRR 1.32\n  [1.10, 1.60]). Grey diamonds are the co-transfer regressor from the co-primary models. Its intervals\n  include 1 on every fold ($p = 0.48$, $0.60$ and $0.053$). The right-hand columns list each estimate with\n  its 95\\% CI and $p$-value.}\n  \\label{fig:grafting}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Robustness.} The co-primary effect holds in 20 of 26 robustness variants on the Screen fold (IRR\nrange 1.11 to 1.56 among significant rows). All seven pre-specified robustness rows on the Held-out fold are\nsignificant. Nativeness-permutation placebos are centred on 1.0 (co-primary $p = 0.002$ Screen, 0.026\nHeld-out, 0.010 MeSH). The cluster-robust variance estimator mildly over-rejects at the null (size 10.5\\% on\nMeSH simulation), so $p$-values should be read alongside the wild-cluster and permutation results.\n\n\\subsubsection{Mechanism decomposition}\n\\label{sec:rq2mechanism}\n\n\\paragraph{Extensive versus intensive margins.} The host-vocabulary effect operates through both the extensive\nmargin, meaning whether any newcomer uptake starts, and the intensive margin, meaning the count of newcomer\npapers given that uptake started. The inverse-variance weighted extensive-margin effect is $+6.4$ percentage\npoints per standard deviation (95\\% CI 4.8 to 8.1, randomisation-$t$ $p < 0.001$), approximately a 13\\%\nincrease relative to the base rate of 51\\%. The inverse-variance weighted intensive-margin incidence-rate ratio\nper standard deviation is 1.18 (95\\% CI 1.10 to 1.27). The extensive share of the total effect is 0.38\n(95\\% CI 0.21 to 0.55; Figure~\\ref{fig:margins}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig5_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Decomposition of the host-vocabulary effect into extensive and intensive margins across the screen,\n  held-out and MeSH folds. Blue circles show per-fold estimates, vermillion diamonds the inverse-variance-weighted\n  (IVW) pooled estimate, and horizontal bars 95\\% confidence intervals. (a)~Extensive margin:\n  linear-probability-model effect of a one-standard-deviation increase in host-vocabulary share on the\n  probability of any newcomer uptake, in percentage points per SD (dashed line: no effect). The pooled effect\n  is 6.43~pp (95\\% CI 4.76 to 8.11). (b)~Intensive margin: PPML incidence-rate ratio per SD conditional on\n  uptake, on a log axis (dashed line: IRR $= 1$). The pooled IRR is 1.183 (95\\% CI 1.104 to 1.267). All three\n  folds are positive on both margins, and every fold interval excludes the null. (c)~Share of the total effect:\n  the extensive margin accounts for 38\\% (95\\% CI 21\\% to 55\\%, black whisker) and the intensive margin for\n  the remaining 62\\%.}\n  \\label{fig:margins}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Host-specific versus generic accessibility.} Adding generality controls (subfield entropy and log\nfrequency of entry partners) to the co-primary model retains 97\\% of the host-vocabulary coefficient\n(inverse-variance weighted retention 0.97, 95\\% CI 0.81 to 1.10), and the Balassa-index lift measure is also\nsignificant (inverse-variance weighted IRR per standard deviation 1.34, 95\\% CI 1.23 to 1.46). The\nhost-vocabulary gradient is not reducible to generic concept accessibility. However, within fixed effects the\nBalassa-index lift measure has a correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share,\nso the lift leg of this test is weak: the two measures carry nearly the same within-unit information, and the\nlift result should be interpreted as confirming the continuous share rather than adding independent evidence\nfor host-specificity.\n\n\\paragraph{No origin-field boundary.} The Wald test for equality of the host-vocabulary effect across\norigin-field groups (Physics and Astronomy, Computer Science, other) is null ($p = 0.64$, label-permutation\n$p = 0.77$). Physics and Astronomy concepts, whose host-vocabulary coefficient is individually non-significant\n(IRR 1.18, 95\\% CI 0.93 to 1.50), fall within sampling variation of the other groups.\n\n\\subsubsection{Diffusion typology and expansion-before-diffusion ordering}\n\\label{sec:rq2typology}\n\nA data-derived typology based on multivariate dynamic time warping of three diversity channels (rarefied\nShannon entropy, Rao-Stirling diversity~\\citep{Stirling2007} and active subfield count) yields a stable\ntwo-cluster solution ($k$-medoids, Hennig bootstrap~\\citep{Hennig2007} minimum Jaccard 0.86):\n\\textbf{localised} ($n = 136$, low entropy and few active subfields) and \\textbf{broad from the start}\n($n = 66$, high entropy from early years). Finer clusterings are unstable ($k = 3$ Jaccard 0.60). The typology\ndoes not separate outcomes better than an entropy-only baseline after residualising on early volume.\n\nAmong concepts exhibiting both a co-word-network expansion onset and a disciplinary-diffusion onset, expansion\nprecedes diffusion in 25 of 26 pooled main-arm cases (proportion 0.96, 95\\% CI 0.81 to 1.00, year-shuffle\nnull 0.62, $p = 0.004$), though only 8.6\\% of concepts have both onsets observable. On MeSH, 9 of 13 show\nexpansion first (not different from the null, $p = 0.43$).\n\n\\subsubsection{Adopter-level mechanism}\n\\label{sec:rq2adopter}\n\nAdopters, defined as authors who publish a concept paper in the host subfield within the five-year outcome\nwindow, are more likely to have prior corpus exposure to the concept's entry partners than matched non-adopters\nfrom the same host subfield (conditional logistic regression: OR 3.09, prevalence 0.79 versus 0.61; 95\\% CI\n2.32 to 4.28; 1,013 matched strata, 422 entries, 109 concepts). Exposure to frequency-matched\nnegative-control concepts is negatively associated (OR 0.62), and the placebo control using partners of a\ndifferent concept's entry into the same host is also below 1 (OR 0.72), showing specificity to the concept's\nown partners.\n\nDecomposing partners into three vocabulary classes --- FOREIGN (origin vocabulary, host share below 5\\%),\nADJACENT (5\\% to 30\\%) and NATIVE (host vocabulary, above 30\\%) --- enrichment follows a gradient: FOREIGN\npartners OR 2.88, ADJACENT partners OR 1.91, NATIVE partners OR 1.47. Adopters who pick up a concept in a new\nfield are most enriched for prior exposure to its origin-vocabulary partners, consistent with the\nabsorptive-capacity framework~\\citep{Cohen1990} in which an individual's ability to recognise and assimilate\nexternal knowledge depends on prior familiarity with that knowledge. This Screen-fold result is not\nindependently confirmed.\n\n\\subsubsection{Comparison to related work}\n\\label{sec:rq2comparison}\n\nOur host-vocabulary measure is closest to the ideational embeddedness of \\citet{Cheng2023}, who found that a\nconcept's fit with existing traditions raises its yearly article count. Their measure is a global property of\nthe concept (mean cosine similarity of all its neighbours in a word2vec embedding), whereas ours is\nentry-specific: measured at the level of each concept-subfield-year event, with concept and host fixed effects\nabsorbing concept-level confounds. Co-transfer, the natural competitor, is null. This extends the principle\nthat relatedness predicts diversification, documented in economic\ngeography~\\citep{Boschma2014, Hidalgo2018}, to the level of individual concept-entry events.\n\nAmong Applied Network Science papers, our work engages most directly with the source-sink analysis of\nknowledge diaspora by \\citet{Domenico2016}, which modelled author flows as diffusion on a bipartite field\nnetwork. Our approach replaces author flows with concept-vocabulary composition at the entry point, and finds\nthat vocabulary, not people, predicts rooting. \\citet{Cunningham2022} documented how multidisciplinary authors\noccupy bridging positions in field-of-study networks, a role that might facilitate the host-vocabulary\ncomposition we measure. \\citet{Fontaine2023} showed that vocabulary overlap between AI and neuroscience\nfacilitated epistemic integration, and our quantitative test provides the micro-level mechanism consistent\nwith their macro-level observation. \\citet{Holmgren2023} developed multilevel alluvial methods for mapping\nchange in higher-order networks, related to the alluvial community tracking we use. \\citet{Medeuov2021}\nappraised discrepancies in semantic networks, finding that endogenous reinforcement within a community is\nweak while exogenous diffusion is predictable, consistent with our expansion-before-diffusion ordering.\n\\citet{Liew2016} applied multiplex network analysis to map disciplinary knowledge flows.\n\n\\subsubsection{Representative cases}\n\\label{sec:rq2cases}\n\nFour medoid cases from the typology clusters illustrate the host-vocabulary gradient at the concept level\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:cases}).\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig6_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Four representative cases of the host-vocabulary gradient. Each panel shows one concept, and each\n  horizontal bar is one of its host entries in the co-primary sample, labelled by host subfield and entry year\n  and sorted by host-vocabulary share (x-axis, fraction). Green bars are rooted entries and grey bars are\n  non-rooted entries. The dashed line marks the mean share of the non-rooted entries, and rooted bars are\n  annotated with their share and number of newcomer papers. (a)~Wireless backhaul (broad, CS): 14 entries, one\n  rooted (Aerospace Engineering 2008, share 0.084, 6 newcomers) against a non-rooted mean of 0.021.\n  (b)~Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen (EPR) steering (broad, Physics): 7 entries, one rooted (Artificial Intelligence\n  2011, 0.142, 37 newcomers; co-transfer 0) against a non-rooted mean of 0.027. (c)~Locally repairable code\n  (localised, CS): a single co-primary entry, rooted (0.056, 3 newcomers), so there is no within-concept\n  contrast. (d)~Holographic QCD (localised, Physics): 5 entries, none rooted (mean 0.041; three have\n  co-transfer 1.0), including an AMO Physics entry at 0.132 that did not take root. In (a) and (b), the rooted\n  entry has a higher host-vocabulary share than every non-rooted entry of the same concept. The panels are\n  descriptive, so no intervals are drawn.}\n  \\label{fig:cases}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Wireless backhaul} (broad type, Computer Science, first appeared 2006). Broad from its first year,\nsplitting between Computer Networks and Electrical Engineering. By 2022 seven subfields are active. Of 14 host\nentries in the co-primary sample, only one is rooted (Aerospace Engineering in 2008, host-vocabulary share\n0.084, 6 newcomer papers). The 13 non-rooted entries average a host-vocabulary share of 0.021 and arrive as\norigin packages (co-transfer 0.6 to 1.0). Rooted-minus-unrooted host-vocabulary share: $+0.062$.\n\n\\paragraph{Einstein--Podolsky--Rosen steering} (broad type, Physics, first appeared 2011). Of 7 co-primary\nentries, one is rooted (Artificial Intelligence in 2011, host-vocabulary share 0.142, co-transfer 0, 37\nnewcomer papers). The 6 non-rooted entries average 0.027 with co-transfer at or above 0.55. Rooted-minus-unrooted:\n$+0.115$. A broad-type label can hide a concept whose cross-disciplinary integration rests on a single\nwell-anchored entry.\n\n\\paragraph{Locally repairable code} (localised type, Computer Science, first appeared 2013). Stays at 84\\% to\n96\\% in Computer Networks for its life. Has only 1 co-primary entry (AI in 2013, host-vocabulary share 0.056,\nrooted). Demonstrates rooting without broad occupancy.\n\n\\paragraph{Holographic QCD} (localised type, Physics, first appeared 2006). Stays at 95\\% to 97\\% in Nuclear\nand High Energy Physics. Its 5 co-primary entries are all non-rooted, averaging 0.041, with three having\nco-transfer of 1.0: pure origin packages. No entry is rooted. A locally concentrated concept whose excursions\nare packaged imports that do not take root.\n\n\\subsection{Community roles and bridging}\n\\label{sec:community}\n\nLeiden community roles (five-seed agreement 97.2\\%) partition concepts into four categories: bridge (0.61),\nother (0.33), stayer (0.03) and migrant (0.02). Emerging concepts are peripheral or connector nodes in the\nGuimera--Amaral cartography~\\citep{Guimera2005a} (peripheral 0.49, connector 0.40, kinless 0.10, no hubs).\nLagged roles do not robustly predict host-subfield entry (bridge odds ratio 0.64, 95\\% CI 0.38 to 1.08).\n\nMost emerging concepts act as bridges between Leiden communities in the co-word network (early-bridging share\n0.70 in the main pool versus 0.59 in MeSH, difference $+0.11$, 95\\% CI 0.02 to 0.20), but this bridging role\nis common and non-discriminating.\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{What host-vocabulary composition tells us}\n\nThe central finding is that a concept's first partners in a new subfield carry information about whether that\nconcept will subsequently be adopted by newcomer scientists in the host field. The host-vocabulary share, a\nratio measuring how much of each partner's prior work belongs to the host subfield, predicts five-year newcomer\nuptake in a pre-registered design replicated on an independent MeSH biomedical population (verdict: REPLICATED),\nwith concordant development-set estimates on the main-arm folds.\n\nThis result complements the absorptive-capacity framework~\\citep{Cohen1990}. At the entry level,\nhost-vocabulary composition facilitates uptake by newcomers who may not be experts in the concept's origin\nfield. At the adopter level, the individuals who actually pick up the concept are enriched for prior exposure\nto the concept's origin-vocabulary partners (OR 3.09, prevalence 0.79 versus 0.61; Screen fold, not\nindependently confirmed), consistent with the proposition that recognising external knowledge requires prior\nfamiliarity with it. These two findings operate at different scales: host-native partners lower the barrier for\nthe field, but the individuals who cross it already speak the origin language.\n\n\\subsection{What structural openness tells us}\n\nThe persistent-neighbour closure result (significant on the Held-out development fold, $S = -1.07$, Holm\n$p = 0.015$) indicates that concepts whose top associates do not close into triads from year to year are more\nlikely to show sustained uptake. General closure is not significant on the Held-out fold. Burt constraint is\npositive, meaning the ego network is redundant, not brokered. The picture is of open, fast-renewing connections\namong a concept's most strongly associated terms within a dense wider ego network, rather than brokerage across\na structural hole. This is consistent with the finding of \\citet{Lin2021} that disconnection and discordance\nseed new directions.\n\n\\subsection{Null findings and what they bound}\n\nSeveral pre-registered hypotheses were not supported. Co-transfer, defined as arriving with origin companions,\nis null in all specifications and populations, meaning that the composition of entry matters but the\nimported-package channel does not. The breadth-prediction screen (does openness predict how many new subfields\na concept will reach?) found no effect beyond growth and level baselines.%\n\\footnote{Code: \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-6}}\nThe link between pre-emergence closure and later host-entry composition is null (partial correlation 0.025\nScreen, 0.053 Held-out, both confidence intervals including zero), meaning that network openness and vocabulary\ncomposition operate independently rather than through a shared mechanism.\n\n\\section{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{Main-arm folds used in development.} The fold labelled Held-out was used during pipeline\ndevelopment: event counts, population sizes and gating decisions were computed on both the Screen and Held-out\nfolds before grafting outcomes were read. Estimates on both main-arm folds are therefore development-set\nestimates, not true held-out confirmations. The independent evidence for the host-vocabulary effect comes from\nthe MeSH replication (verdict: REPLICATED).\n\n\\paragraph{Population bias.} The concept pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science\nconcepts from arXiv. The MeSH population covers only biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries. Generalisation to\nsocial sciences, humanities or engineering is untested.\n\n\\paragraph{Primary specification underpowered.} The fully saturated specification with concept-by-year and\nhost-by-year fixed effects, which absorbs more confounding than the co-primary, is inconclusive on the Held-out\nfold (IRR 0.98, 30 clusters). The independent MeSH replication and the development-set estimates rest on the\nco-primary specification, which leaves more residual variation.\n\n\\paragraph{Single-paper entries.} 87\\% of co-primary Screen events involve a single entry-year paper. The\npooled multi-team effect is positive (IRR 1.28, 95\\% CI 1.11 to 1.48), but the Held-out alone is underpowered\nfor this test.\n\n\\paragraph{Binary establishment null.} The host-vocabulary share predicts the count of newcomer papers and the\nprobability that any newcomer uptake occurs, but binary establishment (at least five newcomer papers in at least\nthree of five years) is null on the Held-out fold ($p = 0.16$). The effect is graded, not threshold-based.\n\n\\paragraph{Cluster-robust inference.} The cluster-robust variance estimator rejects 10\\% to 11\\% of null\nshuffles in simulation (target 5\\%). Wild-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests give consistent results\n(Held-out wild $p = 0.012$, permutation $p = 0.026$), but the standard $p$-values should not be taken at\nface value.\n\n\\paragraph{Host-specificity caveat.} The Balassa-index lift measure used to test host-specificity has a\nwithin-fixed-effect correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share. The lift test\nconfirms the continuous measure rather than providing independent evidence.\n\n\\paragraph{Screen-fold adopter evidence.} The adopter-level enrichment (OR 3.09) is Screen-fold only, not\nindependently confirmed. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.\n\n\\paragraph{Closure Held-out caveats.} The Held-out fold was used in pipeline development, so the closure\nresult is a development-set estimate. Additionally, the Held-out matching falls back to Screen controls for\n17 of 25 unique controls, so the estimator is not fully control-side independent. The MeSH closure result is\ndirectional under the sensitivity label but null under the primary label.\n\n\\section{Conclusions}\n\\label{sec:conclusions}\n\nWhen a new scientific concept enters a disciplinary subfield, the vocabulary composition of its initial\npartners predicts whether newcomer scientists in that field will subsequently adopt it. This host-vocabulary\neffect, replicated on 191 independent MeSH biomedical concepts (co-primary IRR 1.23, verdict REPLICATED)\nwith concordant main-arm development-set estimates (Screen IRR 1.30, Held-out IRR 1.19), is host-specific\n--- though the Balassa-index lift leg of this test is near-collinear with the continuous share\n(within-fixed-effect $r = 0.997$) --- operates through both the extensive and intensive margins, and does\nnot vary by the concept's origin field. Co-transfer of origin companions is null.\n\nThe complementary structural finding, that persistent-neighbour closure is lower before sustained uptake\n(Held-out development-set estimate $S = -1.07$, Holm $p = 0.015$) while Burt constraint is higher, provides\nthe network context: emerging concepts sit in locally open, fast-renewing neighbourhoods that span multiple\ncommunities but are not brokered in Burt's sense.\n\nThese results bear on how knowledge transfer is evaluated and supported. Policies and platforms that facilitate\ncross-disciplinary research might benefit from attending to the vocabulary composition of a concept's first\nappearance in a new field, rather than only to the mobility of authors who carry it.\n\nFuture work should extend the concept pool beyond the physical and computational sciences, test whether the\nhost-vocabulary gradient holds for social-science and humanities concepts, and design an experiment to separate\nabsorptive capacity from topical proximity at the adopter level.\n\n\\section*{Declarations}\n\n\\paragraph{Funding.} Not applicable.\n\n\\paragraph{Conflicts of interest.} The authors declare no conflicts of interest.\n\n\\paragraph{Availability of data and materials.} All data derive from OpenAlex, an open scholarly metadata\nindex. The concept pool, verified work lists and analysis code are available in the project repository.\n\n\\paragraph{Code availability.} All analysis code is available in the project repository.\n\n\\paragraph{Keywords.} Knowledge diffusion, emerging concepts, co-word network, host vocabulary,\ncross-disciplinary integration, applied network science, scientometrics, concept emergence.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 697, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 697}}

<!-- HERO -->
<section class="hero" id="hero">
<h1>Host vocabulary predicts whether new scientific concepts take root across disciplinary boundaries</h1>

<p class="tldr">When a new scientific concept first appears in a disciplinary subfield, does the vocabulary of its initial partner terms predict whether newcomer scientists will adopt it? Across 426 emerging concepts and 462,812 works from OpenAlex, the answer is yes: a one-standard-deviation increase in the share of entry partners belonging to the host field's vocabulary raises five-year newcomer uptake by 23% (incidence-rate ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.36), replicated on an independent population of 191 MeSH biomedical concepts.</p>

<a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new@fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/paper.pdf">Read the paper (PDF)</a>

</section>

<!-- CONTRIBUTIONS -->
<section id="contributions">
<h2>Contributions</h2>
<div class="cards">

<div class="card">
<h3>Host-entry grafting predicts adoption</h3>
<p>When a concept enters a new subfield, the share of its entry partners belonging to the host vocabulary predicts five-year newcomer uptake. Pre-registered and replicated on an independent MeSH biomedical population (co-primary IRR 1.23, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.36; verdict: REPLICATED). Development-set estimates are concordant: Screen IRR 1.30, Held-out IRR 1.19.</p>
<div class="cl">
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-7">Code: Do borrowed ideas stick when grafted locally?</a>
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-2">Code: One-time held-out check of the idea-grafting result</a>
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/experiment-9">Code: Idea grafting replicates in biomedical MeSH concepts</a>
</div>
</div>

<div class="card">
<h3>Outcome-blind concept dataset</h3>
<p>A semantically grounded, outcome-blind dataset of 426 emerging concepts with 462,812 OpenAlex works across physics, computer science and biomedicine, plus an independent check population of 191 MeSH biomedical concepts.</p>
<div class="cl">
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-1/dataset-1">Code: New science concepts and their papers</a>
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/dataset-5">Code: All concept papers downloaded, with field labels</a>
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-1/dataset-3">Code: New MeSH medical terms as a held-out check set</a>
</div>
</div>

<div class="card">
<h3>Host-specific effect through two margins</h3>
<p>The host-vocabulary effect is host-specific rather than a proxy for generic concept accessibility, and it operates through both the extensive margin (whether uptake starts, +6.4 pp per SD) and the intensive margin (its magnitude, IRR 1.18). No detectable variation by origin field.</p>
<div class="cl">
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-5/evaluation-6">Code: Does host vocabulary start uptake or grow it?</a>
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-5/evaluation-7">Code: Host-specific or just common words?</a>
</div>
</div>

<div class="card">
<h3>Structural precursors of emergence</h3>
<p>Persistent-neighbour closure is lower before sustained uptake (S = &#x2212;1.07, Holm p = 0.015; development-set estimate). General closure fails on the Held-out fold. The effect is not Burt brokerage: emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not less constrained, ego networks.</p>
<div class="cl">
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-5">Code: Is openness before take-off brokerage or churn?</a>
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-3">Code: One-time held-out check of closure and D3 link</a>
</div>
</div>

<div class="card">
<h3>Diffusion typology and adopter enrichment</h3>
<p>A stable two-type typology (localised vs. broad), an expansion-before-diffusion ordering (25 of 26 cases), and adopter-level enrichment for prior exposure to the concept's entry partners (OR 3.09; Screen fold, not independently confirmed).</p>
<div class="cl">
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-8">Code: How new concepts spread: types, roles, timing</a>
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-4">Code: Checking concept spread types on unseen and medical data</a>
<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-5">Code: Do adopters already know the partner words?</a>
</div>
</div>

</div>
</section>

<!-- METHOD -->
<section id="method">
<h2>Method</h2>

<figure>
<img class="method-fig" src="figures/fig1_v0.jpg"
  alt="Study design diagram with four panels: data sources showing 426 arXiv concepts split into screen and held-out folds plus 191 MeSH concepts drawn from 462,812 OpenAlex works; co-word network of 25 yearly snapshots with approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges with Leiden communities; RQ1 matched event study comparing closure before sustained uptake; RQ2 host-entry grafting measuring host-vocabulary share to predict newcomer uptake"
  tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Enlarge Figure 1: Study design and analysis pipeline"
  data-lb-src="figures/fig1_v0.jpg"
  data-lb-title="Figure 1. Study design and analysis pipeline">
<figcaption style="font-size:14px;color:var(--text-sec);margin-top:8px;">
<strong style="font-size:15px;color:var(--text);display:block;margin-bottom:2px;">Figure 1. Study design and analysis pipeline</strong>
</figcaption>
</figure>

<h3>Data</h3>
<p>The study tracks 426 emerging scientific concepts, assembled as an outcome-blind pool from arXiv noun phrases that first appeared in OpenAlex between 2005 and 2016 (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-1/dataset-1">code</a>). Of these, 366 are main emerging concepts (247 Screen fold, 119 Held-out fold) and 60 are stationary references. A logistic-regression classifier (F1 = 0.82, AUC = 0.89) and a variant merger (B-cubed F1 = 0.78) grounded every concept (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/experiment-1">code</a>). The pool is dominated by physics and computer-science concepts from arXiv.</p>

<p>An independent biomedical arm of 191 concepts was drawn from new MeSH descriptors (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-1/dataset-3">code</a>). The combined corpus comprises 462,812 unique OpenAlex works (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/dataset-5">code</a>).</p>

<h3>Co-word network</h3>
<p>From a design-weighted background sample of 259,716 works, 25 yearly three-year-window co-occurrence snapshots were built (approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges per snapshot), with association-strength edge weights and Leiden community detection (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/experiment-3">code</a>). For each concept-keyword node, OpenAlex subfield-by-time-block publication counts supplied the host-vocabulary share used in RQ2, covering 78.7% of host co-occurrence weight across 1,372 nodes.</p>

<h3>RQ1: Structural precursors of emergence</h3>
<p>Sustained uptake is defined as reaching at least 20 papers per year with at least 20 percentile points of co-word network strength gain. Each concept showing sustained uptake is matched 1:1 to a control from the same first-appearance band and origin field. The standardised mean difference (Cohen's S) in closure measures during the pre-onset window is the estimand, with bootstrap confidence intervals (B = 2,000) and Holm-corrected p-values. Four closure variants were tested: general closure, turnover-residualised closure, persistent-neighbour closure (restricted to top-20 neighbours present in consecutive years), and Burt constraint.</p>

<h3>RQ2: Host-entry grafting</h3>
<p>A host-entry event is the first year a concept appears in a non-origin subfield together with at least five co-occurring partner terms. The host-vocabulary share measures the tag-weighted mean of each partner's pre-entry publication share in the host subfield. The outcome is five-year newcomer uptake: host-subfield papers by author-disjoint newcomers.</p>

<p>Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML) regression with concept-clustered standard errors tests whether host-vocabulary share predicts uptake. Two specifications were pre-registered: a primary with concept&#xD7;year and host&#xD7;year fixed effects, and a co-primary with concept, entry-year and host fixed effects (used when the primary drops below 30 concept clusters). Co-transfer (fraction of partners that were origin companions) is included as a second regressor in both.</p>
</section>

<!-- RESULTS -->
<section id="results">
<h2>Results</h2>

<h3>Host-entry grafting</h3>

<div class="res">
<div class="res-label">MeSH replication (independent)</div>
<div class="res-num">IRR 1.23</div>
<div class="res-ctx">95% CI 1.12 to 1.36, p &lt; 0.001. Co-primary specification on 191 independent MeSH biomedical concepts (2,171 events, 160 concept clusters). Pre-registered verdict: REPLICATED. The primary specification is also significant (IRR 1.32, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.60, p = 0.004).</div>
</div>

<div class="res">
<div class="res-label">Screen fold (development set)</div>
<div class="res-num">IRR 1.30</div>
<div class="res-ctx">95% CI 1.16 to 1.45, p &lt; 0.001. Co-primary specification, 1,544 events across 140 concept clusters.</div>
</div>

<div class="res">
<div class="res-label">Held-out fold (development set)</div>
<div class="res-num">IRR 1.19</div>
<div class="res-ctx">95% CI 1.06 to 1.33, p = 0.004. Co-primary specification, 972 events across 74 concept clusters. Wild-cluster bootstrap p = 0.012, nativeness-permutation p = 0.026. The fully saturated primary specification is inconclusive (IRR 0.98, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.37, 30 clusters, p = 0.91), declared underpowered in advance.</div>
</div>

<div class="res">
<div class="res-label">Pooled estimate (IVW, all three folds)</div>
<div class="res-num">IRR 1.26</div>
<div class="res-ctx">95% CI 1.17 to 1.36, I&sup2; = 0. One standard deviation of host-vocabulary share raises newcomer uptake by 26%.</div>
</div>

<div class="res">
<div class="res-label">Co-transfer</div>
<div class="res-num">Null</div>
<div class="res-ctx">Null across all folds and specifications (p = 0.48, 0.60, and 0.053). Arriving with origin companions does not predict uptake.</div>
</div>

<h3>Margin decomposition</h3>
<p>The host-vocabulary effect operates through both margins (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-5/evaluation-6">code</a>). The extensive margin (whether any uptake starts) accounts for 38% of the total effect (95% CI 21% to 55%): the pooled effect is +6.4 percentage points per SD (95% CI 4.8 to 8.1), approximately a 13% increase relative to the 51% base rate. The intensive margin (count of newcomer papers given uptake started) accounts for the remaining 62%, with a pooled IRR of 1.18 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.27).</p>

<p>The host-vocabulary gradient is host-specific. Adding generality controls retains 97% of the coefficient (IVW retention 0.97, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.10). The Balassa-index lift measure is also significant (IVW IRR 1.34, 95% CI 1.23 to 1.46), though its within-fixed-effect correlation with the log of the continuous share is 0.997, so the lift test confirms the continuous measure rather than adding independent evidence (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-5/evaluation-7">code</a>). The Wald test for origin-field dependence is null (p = 0.64).</p>

<h3>Structural precursors of emergence</h3>
<p>On the Held-out fold (a development-set estimate), only persistent-neighbour closure survives Holm correction: S = &#x2212;1.07, 95% CI &#x2212;1.86 to &#x2212;0.29, Holm p = 0.015. General closure is not significant (Holm p = 0.147). Turnover-residualised closure is not significant (Holm p = 0.635). Burt constraint is positive (S = +0.11, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.19), indicating that emerging concepts sit in more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-5">code</a>, <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-3">held-out check</a>).</p>

<p>The MeSH replication of closure is directional under a sensitivity label (D = &#x2212;0.42, Holm p = 0.039, n = 29) but null under the primary label (D = &#x2212;0.09, Holm p = 0.677, n = 15) (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-2/experiment-4">code</a>). Structural precursors add no predictive value for sustained uptake beyond frequency, burst, degree and entropy baselines (logistic AUC 0.89 versus 0.88).</p>

<h3>Adopter-level mechanism</h3>
<p>Adopters are more likely to have prior corpus exposure to the concept's entry partners than matched non-adopters (conditional logistic regression: OR 3.09, prevalence 0.79 versus 0.61; 95% CI 2.32 to 4.28; 1,013 matched strata, 422 entries, 109 concepts; Screen fold, not independently confirmed) (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-5">code</a>). Enrichment follows a vocabulary gradient: FOREIGN partners OR 2.88, ADJACENT OR 1.91, NATIVE OR 1.47.</p>

<h3>Diffusion typology</h3>
<p>A data-derived two-type typology (localised, n = 136, vs. broad from the start, n = 66; k-medoids, bootstrap minimum Jaccard 0.86) is stable, though it does not separate outcomes better than an entropy-only baseline. Among concepts with both observable onsets, expansion precedes diffusion in 25 of 26 pooled main-arm cases (proportion 0.96, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.00, p = 0.004) (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-8">code</a>, <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-4/evaluation-4">unseen data check</a>).</p>

<h3>Null findings</h3>
<p>Co-transfer is null in all specifications and populations. The breadth-prediction screen (does openness predict how many subfields a concept reaches?) found no effect beyond growth and level baselines (<a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-8892b7-occupancy-is-not-integration-for-new/tree/fork/run_YczZzZ0_9kfq/round-3/experiment-6">code</a>). The link between pre-emergence closure and later host-entry composition is null (partial correlation 0.025 Screen, 0.053 Held-out, both CIs including zero).</p>
</section>

<!-- FIGURES -->
<section id="figures">
<h2>Figures</h2>
<div class="gallery">

<div class="gal-item" tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Enlarge Figure 1: Study design and analysis pipeline" data-lb-src="figures/fig1_v0.jpg" data-lb-title="Figure 1. Study design and analysis pipeline">
<img src="figures/fig1_v0.jpg" alt="Study design diagram with four panels: data sources, co-word network, matched event study for RQ1, and host-entry grafting framework for RQ2" loading="lazy">
<div class="gal-cap"><span class="gal-title">Figure 1. Study design and analysis pipeline</span>
Overview of the study design. (a) Data: an outcome-blind arXiv concept pool of 426 emerging scientific concepts, split into a screen fold (247) and a held-out fold (119), and an independent MeSH biomedical check population of 191 concepts. Both are drawn from 462,812 OpenAlex works. (b) Co-word network: yearly co-word snapshots (25 snapshots, ~27k nodes, ~84k edges) with Leiden communities. (c) RQ1, emergence precursors: a matched event study compares closure measures in the pre-onset window between concepts showing sustained uptake (blue, rising) and controls (grey, flat). (d) RQ2, host-entry grafting: a concept enters a non-origin host subfield; the host-vocabulary share is the exposure in a pre-registered PPML regression predicting 5-year newcomer uptake. The timelines and bars in (c) and (d) are schematic and carry no data values.</div>
</div>

<div class="gal-item" tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Enlarge Figure 2: Co-word network snapshot" data-lb-src="figures/fig2_v0.jpg" data-lb-title="Figure 2. Co-word network snapshot">
<img src="figures/fig2_v0.jpg" alt="Co-word network visualization showing six coloured Leiden communities with pool concepts at community peripheries, three labeled: wireless backhaul, EPR steering, holographic QCD" loading="lazy">
<div class="gal-cap"><span class="gal-title">Figure 2. Co-word network snapshot</span>
Schematic co-word network snapshot (2012, three-year window). Nodes are concept-keyword terms and grey edges are association-strength weighted co-occurrences; node fill colour (blue, green, orange, purple, red, teal) marks Leiden community membership, and larger circles are high-degree hub terms. Pool concepts (bold black rings) sit on the periphery of communities, mostly in the gaps between two of them, where they act as bridge or connector nodes; three are labelled (wireless backhaul, EPR steering, holographic QCD). The full network comprises approximately 27,000 nodes and 84,000 edges; the panel is an illustrative rendering of its high-degree core.</div>
</div>

<div class="gal-item" tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Enlarge Figure 3: Pre-emergence closure by measure type" data-lb-src="figures/fig3_v0.png" data-lb-title="Figure 3. Pre-emergence closure by measure type">
<img src="figures/fig3_v0.png" alt="Forest plot of four closure measures on the held-out fold: only persistent-neighbour closure (blue, S = negative 1.07) survives Holm correction; general closure and turnover-residualised closure shown in grey cross zero; Burt constraint in orange is positive at 0.11" loading="lazy">
<div class="gal-cap"><span class="gal-title">Figure 3. Pre-emergence closure by measure type</span>
Pre-emergence closure on the held-out fold. Each row shows the standardised mean difference (S) between concepts that later show sustained uptake and matched controls. Points are estimates and horizontal bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Only persistent-neighbour closure (blue) survives Holm correction (S = &#x2212;1.07, 95% CI [&#x2212;1.86, &#x2212;0.29], Holm p = 0.015). General closure (Holm p = 0.147) and turnover-residualised closure (Holm p = 0.635) are shown in grey. Burt constraint (orange) is positive (S = 0.11, 95% CI [0.02, 0.19]), indicating more constrained, not more brokered, ego networks.</div>
</div>

<div class="gal-item" tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Enlarge Figure 4: Host-vocabulary effect across folds" data-lb-src="figures/fig4_v0.png" data-lb-title="Figure 4. Host-vocabulary effect across folds">
<img src="figures/fig4_v0.png" alt="Forest plot of host-vocabulary incidence-rate ratios across screen, held-out, and MeSH folds showing co-primary IRRs of 1.30, 1.19, and 1.23 respectively, with pooled IVW estimate of 1.26, and null co-transfer on all folds" loading="lazy">
<div class="gal-cap"><span class="gal-title">Figure 4. Host-vocabulary effect across folds</span>
Host-vocabulary effect on five-year newcomer uptake across folds and specifications. Each row gives the PPML incidence-rate ratio (IRR) per one standard deviation of host-vocabulary share, on a log axis. Filled circles are the co-primary specification, open circles the primary specification. Blue marks the OpenAlex folds, green the independent MeSH replication, and the amber diamond the IVW pooled co-primary estimate. The co-primary effect is significant on all three folds (screen IRR 1.30 [1.16, 1.45], held-out 1.19 [1.06, 1.33], MeSH 1.23 [1.12, 1.36]), and the pooled estimate is 1.26 [1.17, 1.36]. Grey diamonds are the co-transfer regressor; its intervals include 1 on every fold.</div>

<div class="gal-item" tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Enlarge Figure 5: Extensive and intensive margin decomposition" data-lb-src="figures/fig5_v0.png" data-lb-title="Figure 5. Extensive and intensive margin decomposition">
<img src="figures/fig5_v0.png" alt="Three-panel decomposition: extensive margin shows pooled effect of 6.43 percentage points; intensive margin shows pooled IRR of 1.183; share bar shows 38% extensive and 62% intensive" loading="lazy">
<div class="gal-cap"><span class="gal-title">Figure 5. Extensive and intensive margin decomposition</span>
Decomposition of the host-vocabulary effect across the screen, held-out and MeSH folds. Blue circles show per-fold estimates, vermillion diamonds the IVW pooled estimate. (a) Extensive margin: the pooled effect is 6.43 pp (95% CI 4.76 to 8.11). (b) Intensive margin: the pooled IRR is 1.183 (95% CI 1.104 to 1.267). All three folds are positive on both margins, and every fold interval excludes the null. (c) The extensive margin accounts for 38% (95% CI 21% to 55%) and the intensive margin for the remaining 62%.</div>
</div>

<img src="figures/fig6_v0.png" alt="Four bar-chart panels showing host-vocabulary share for representative concepts: wireless backhaul with one rooted entry at 0.084, EPR steering with one rooted entry at 0.142, locally repairable code with a single rooted entry at 0.056, and holographic QCD with no rooted entries" loading="lazy">
<div class="gal-cap"><span class="gal-title">Figure 6. Four representative cases</span>
Four representative cases of the host-vocabulary gradient. Green bars are rooted entries and grey bars are non-rooted entries. (a) Wireless backhaul (broad, CS): 14 entries, one rooted (Aerospace Engineering 2008, share 0.084, 6 newcomers) against a non-rooted mean of 0.021. (b) EPR steering (broad, Physics): 7 entries, one rooted (Artificial Intelligence 2011, 0.142, 37 newcomers; co-transfer 0) against a non-rooted mean of 0.027. (c) Locally repairable code (localised, CS): a single co-primary entry, rooted (0.056, 3 newcomers). (d) Holographic QCD (localised, Physics): 5 entries, none rooted (mean 0.041). In (a) and (b), the rooted entry has a higher host-vocabulary share than every non-rooted entry.</div>

<!-- LIMITATIONS -->
<section id="limitations">
<h2>Limitations</h2>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Main-arm folds used in development</strong>
<p>The Held-out fold was used during pipeline development: event counts, population sizes and gating decisions were computed on both folds before grafting outcomes were read. Estimates on both main-arm folds are development-set estimates, not true held-out confirmations. The independent evidence comes from the MeSH replication.</p>
</div>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Population bias</strong>
<p>The concept pool is dominated by physics, physical-sciences and computer-science concepts from arXiv. The MeSH population covers only biomedicine-to-biomedicine entries. Generalisation to social sciences, humanities or engineering is untested.</p>
</div>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Primary specification underpowered</strong>
<p>The fully saturated specification with concept&#xD7;year and host&#xD7;year fixed effects is inconclusive on the Held-out fold (IRR 0.98, 30 clusters). The MeSH replication and development-set estimates rest on the co-primary specification, which absorbs less confounding.</p>
</div>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Single-paper entries</strong>
<p>87% of co-primary Screen events involve a single entry-year paper. The pooled multi-team effect is positive (IRR 1.28, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.48), but the Held-out fold alone is underpowered for this test.</p>
</div>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Binary establishment null</strong>
<p>Host-vocabulary share predicts the count of newcomer papers and the probability of any uptake, but binary establishment (at least five newcomer papers in at least three of five years) is null on the Held-out fold (p = 0.16). The effect is graded, not threshold-based.</p>
</div>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Cluster-robust inference</strong>
<p>The cluster-robust variance estimator rejects 10% to 11% of null shuffles in simulation (target 5%). Wild-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests give consistent results (Held-out wild p = 0.012, permutation p = 0.026), but standard p-values should not be taken at face value.</p>
</div>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Host-specificity caveat</strong>
<p>The Balassa-index lift measure has a within-fixed-effect correlation of 0.997 with the log of the continuous host-vocabulary share. The lift test confirms the continuous measure rather than providing independent evidence for host-specificity.</p>
</div>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Adopter evidence not confirmed</strong>
<p>The adopter-level enrichment (OR 3.09) is Screen-fold only, not independently confirmed. The design cannot separate absorptive capacity from topical proximity.</p>
</div>

<div class="lim">
<strong>Closure caveats</strong>
<p>The Held-out fold was used in pipeline development, so the closure result is a development-set estimate. The Held-out matching falls back to Screen controls for 17 of 25 unique controls. The MeSH closure result is directional under the sensitivity label but null under the primary label.</p>
</div>
</section>

}\n.gal-item:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset: 4px; border-radius: 3px; }\n.gal-cap { font-size: 14px; color: var(--text-sec); margin-top: 10px; line-height: 1.55; max-width: 68ch; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;\n  transition: background .15s;\n}\n.lb-close:hover { background: rgba(255,255,255,.3); }\n.lb-close:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #fff; outline-offset: 2px; }\n.lb-cap { color: #ccc; font-size: 14px; margin-top: 12px; text-align: center; max-width: 80ch; line-height: 1.5; max-height: 15vh; overflow-y: auto; padding: 0 16px; }\n\n/* Limitations */\n.lim { margin-bottom: 20px;
